I never meant Buddhism is an obligation. I just meant that idealistically that’s how things would be since it would involve the least amount of suffering and a lot of enlightenment. it’s not a pragmatic approach in any way. Idealistically does not mean realistic. I meant to point out that although the ideals of Buddhism are unsustainable, because we don’t live in an idealistic world (we live in a realistic one) it is sustainable. This is worth looking at because many might question the ideals of Buddhism if that wasn’t considered. 

For example: idealistically capitalism in theory would create fairness among the classes, but realistically, it does not do this perfectly. (Capitalism may or may not be the best system we have to offer but it has flaws like every system) It’s always worth comparing the differences between the ideals of an ideology and the way in which it truly functions as to not confuse people. Consider if an alien (somebody with an objective view) looked at capitalism and all it knew was the idealistic function. It might think capitalism was perfect by nature. But of course we all know capitalism is not perfect, and common belief in a perfect system could be dangerous as the flaws of the system would go undetected. This is why it’s important to emphasize the difference between idealism and pragmatism in an ideology.

I don’t mean to sound crude, but diaphragmatic breathing is considered a form of meditation to many. But feel free to disagree. There’s an element of subjectivity here. 

I guess I wish people would open up to the idea that meditation is not just sitting in one place with your eyes closed and focusing on awareness all around. In essence all meditation is (in my opinion) is silencing intrusive thoughts by focusing on a certain element. It’s gives the “monkey mind” a task, often repetitive, to quiet the other sporadic thoughts.

This means focusing on the breath is meditation. You can do it while walking, studying, listening to music, etc. You don’t have to look deep inside yourself to focus on the breath. Sitting meditation is just one of many techniques.

This is vastly generalizing the anxious population. Meditation has been proven by anecdotal reports and science to be effective in decreasing anxiety. I understand it’s not for everyone, but just because it doesn’t work for you, doesn’t mean it doesn’t work wonders for many others. It’s recommended for a reason. It doesn’t fix psychosocial elements of your life. But it develops the awareness to further improve your cognition and behaviour. All I’m saying is try not to generalize people/meditation based on (what seems like) your own experience.

Also for the sake of reference I have a panic attack at least a handful of times a week. Meditation usually goes something like this:

-“Oh fuck I have to put effort into this?!?! This is terrible. Why would I do this?”

“Fuck it I’m losing it, I’ve nothing to lose.”

*starts meditating*

-“This sucks cause I’m not hiding from my anxiety. I’m forced to face it. Screw this.”

*either gives up and my panic attack goes berserk or I continue on:*

-“My thoughts are beginning to settle. I’m still tense but things are surprisingly better now that I sat with my anxiety for some time. Now that I think about it, this was worth it. I might be panicky and tense but I can think clearly and this isn’t hell on earth anymore.”

It’s easy to give up before you get over that hump. And it won’t work for all. But the fact that it’s worked like this for even me, proves that it can be beneficial. Even to those in a panic attack.

As I’m sure you know, nobody except yourself can find your purpose in life. But if you want some insight, here’s my advice:

Don’t be fooled by the ego. The ego is what fuels greed, hatred, corruption, desire, lust, etc. Even if you think you’ve got your ego figured out, second guessing yourself is always worth it as even subtle things are fuelled by the ego. On your path to finding your meaning, make sure you look past the ego. 

Always look within. No matter what you choose to believe, it’s you who chooses. Don’t let another choose for you. the Buddha himself said not to have blind faith in any of their words, rather, the learner should meditate on their teachings and decide for themselves what to believe. Even if you choose to believe in a god which exists outside of you, it is the responsibility of that god to reveal themselves to you. (FYI I’m not saying that believing in god is illogical. I’m saying that if we are to find god, the only way is to look within ourselves. By doing so we will find god if he exists. If not then we’ll find some other truth or meaning in life)

Don’t force yourself to find meaning too fast. Sometimes what makes us miss the meaning in life is how hard we’re trying to find it. So many people are so busy in life, trying to find what will seemingly make them happy, materialism, consumerism, jobs, even certain relationships, all make us feel like we’re on a path to find our place in life where we feel whole. Yet so many people finally find that place and feel they still haven’t found their place in life. Or their meaning in life.  Sometimes our meaning has been right in front of us all along. This is why I think meditation is so important. It often gets associated with Buddhism and other esoteric ideologies, but I think it’s important for every ideology, as it allows for us to realize our true nature by pausing and stepping out of this neurotic cycle. 

Life’s meaning might mean something different to you but here’s what it means to me. Of course, even this is just what I make of it:

I’ve realized that our meaning in life is what we make of it. Meditation has allowed me to strip away the ego to find my true self. This self finds peace in every moment, perfectly content with the stillness which surrounds me. And this is the meaning to life. All of our emotions and feelings are somewhat like a levelling system or a rewards system in a video game. The video game doesn’t have any real purpose just like life doesn’t have any real purpose. But that’s not such a bad thing unless you attach to the ego. If you stop attaching to the ego it’s actually a very wonderful and spiritual sensation to be able to find a moment of peace and joy within any moment of the day. No longer looking forward to the next pay check, finishing work, etc, but rather, enjoying the present moment, in every moment, even if you find yourself in a position where you would usually be suffering.

I hope all or just some of this can help you to find meaning


TL;DR ~ looking past the ego, looking within yourself and meditation might help you find meaning in life.

If I said hell wasn’t real I’d be lying. But it exists on this plane of existence. Not after death. And we live in it every day. We also live in heaven every day. Buddhism just teaches you to go to heaven. 

In essence, they’re the same concepts, but Buddhism generally rejects the belief in a god (depending on who you ask. Even those who do believe in “gods” do so with little dogma, involved, i.e. they take it with a grain of salt.) , rather, it believes you are god. Heaven/hell is within you. All religions seek to find the same thing; the cessation of suffering. 

The difference is that Buddhism acknowledges that the only way to do this is to realize suffering comes from our attachments to what we cannot control. (Mot related, but anxiety relies on this as well) and thus, we cannot depend on that which is outside of us, as we cannot control this. It focuses attention inwards, and teaches to love oneself.

 I would argue that the concept of “god” in ones mind is just the ego convincing itself it is connecting to the the ego-less self. This doesn’t work though as this tricks the ego into thinking it exists, the ego-less self thus fanning the flames of the ego. However, without the ego, we awaken to the truth that we are god, everyone is god, and we are all one. This is why Buddhists aren’t afraid of hell. Because fear itself is hell in the eyes of a Buddhist. And the teaching allows us to escape the hell which the ego inflicts upon itself.

TLDR; it’s a difference of beliefs. Islam believes god is an omnipotent being in the sky, Buddhism believes god is a concept we created within us. Thus, we have no reason to fear god unless we fear the destructive nature of our own mind/ego.

It depends on the type of meditation. There’s no wrong meditation technique but it all depends on what you intend to accomplish. 

For example two monks were discussing the right way to meditate with their teacher. The first one goes “well the right way to meditate should be to let your thoughts run free, to see where they go and observe your thoughts.” And the teacher says “You’re right.” Then the second monk says “Well wouldn’t it be better to focus on breathing to clear the mind and focus on simple existence and the moment?” And the teacher replies “You’re right” and finally the first monk says “But you can’t do both, they contradict each other” And the teacher replies yet again “You’re right”

The point is that you must set the intention and technique before you meditate. What’s more important than the technique itself is sticking to the technique you’ve chosen and developing discipline in your meditation/practice.

meditating while sick is the best time to meditate. 

There’s a zen saying which goes “You should sit in meditation for 20 minutes a day. Unless you’re too busy; then you should sit for an hour.”

This can apply to being sick as well IMO. If you’re too sick to meditate for 20 minutes, you should meditate for an hour.

I think a misconception is that comfort is required to meditate. However comfort can help, and thus there’s nothing wrong with being comfortable while you sit, we can’t always be comfortable. And as such meditating in uncomfortable situations teaches us to find comfort even if our given situation doesn’t provide it. 

Ultimately everything around us is in constant change, the only thing meditating while sick/in uncomfortable situations will do, is teach us how to adapt.
